query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of tungsten (about 0.5 at.%) to the CoCrFeNi matrix will induce the formation of W-rich intermetallic phases and adaptive near-surface oxide/nanocrystalline layers during sliding, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Alloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with approximately 0.5 at.% tungsten.
generation.conditions: Sliding friction tests conducted under controlled loads and atmospheric (oxidative) conditions with temperatures varied incrementally from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds and an adaptive, ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer (which may include reactive oxides) at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: W addition enhances lattice distortion and triggers phase transformations upon wear; under sliding, the W-rich phases organize into a robust surface layer that counteracts abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear, thus providing adaptive friction interface protection.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unalloyed CoCrFeNi, the W-alloyed HEA is predicted to exhibit a significantly lower and more stable coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range, particularly improving high-temperature performance.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which shows increased friction and wear challenges when subjected to high-temperature sliding.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective in ambient (oxidative) environments under sliding loads typical of tribological tests, and within the temperature range of room temperature to 800 °C; its effectiveness under extreme loads or non-standard atmospheres remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate has not been determined, and may depend on processing conditions, tungsten distribution, and the precise nature of the tribolayer formed during sliding.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) baseline CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy and (2) CoCrFeNi alloy with 0.5 at.% tungsten. Under identical experimental conditions, perform sliding wear tests across a range of temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C. Control parameters such as load, sliding distance, and environment. Periodically characterize the near-surface microstructure (using SEM, TEM, and XRD) to confirm the formation of W-rich phases and adaptive layers.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding across the temperature range
Microstructural analysis of the wear track to identify phase transformations and tribolayer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-alloyed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in the coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy across the temperature range, or if no adaptive tribolayer or W-rich phases are formed during sliding, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Reactive wear protection through strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces

Abstract: Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. The reactive wear protection strategy offers a pathway for designing ultra-wear resistant alloys

Effects of W Alloying on the Lattice Distortion and Wear Behavior of Laser Cladding AlCoCrFeNiWx High-Entropy Alloy Coatings

Abstract: AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS).
